front_blocks.md: Define **cerebral hemispheres**.

back_blocks.md: The **cerebral hemispheres** are the two halves of the largest part of the brain, controlling **conscious activities** such as vision, hearing, speech, thinking and memory.

cards.front_md: Define **cerebral hemispheres**.
cards.back_md: The **cerebral hemispheres** are the two halves of the largest part of the brain, controlling **conscious activities** such as vision, hearing, speech, thinking and memory.

front_blocks.md: Define **hypothalamus**.

back_blocks.md: The **hypothalamus** monitors the blood flowing through the brain and, in response, **releases hormones** or stimulates the **pituitary gland**, playing a key role in **homeostasis** (e.g. body temperature and water balance).

cards.front_md: Define **hypothalamus**.
cards.back_md: The **hypothalamus** monitors the blood flowing through the brain and, in response, **releases hormones** or stimulates the **pituitary gland**, playing a key role in **homeostasis** (e.g. body temperature and water balance).

front_blocks.md: Define **pituitary gland**.

back_blocks.md: The **pituitary gland**, located below the hypothalamus, produces a range of **hormones**, some acting directly on the body and others stimulating **other endocrine glands** to release their hormones.

cards.front_md: Define **pituitary gland**.
cards.back_md: The **pituitary gland**, located below the hypothalamus, produces a range of **hormones**, some acting directly on the body and others stimulating **other endocrine glands** to release their hormones.

front_blocks.md: Define **cerebellum**.

back_blocks.md: The **cerebellum** coordinates **movement** and **balance**, controlling muscle activity to produce smooth, coordinated actions.

cards.front_md: Define **cerebellum**.
cards.back_md: The **cerebellum** coordinates **movement** and **balance**, controlling muscle activity to produce smooth, coordinated actions.

front_blocks.md: Define **medulla oblongata**.

back_blocks.md: The **medulla oblongata** contains coordination centres that control **unconscious functions** such as **heart rate** and **breathing rate**.

cards.front_md: Define **medulla oblongata**.
cards.back_md: The **medulla oblongata** contains coordination centres that control **unconscious functions** such as **heart rate** and **breathing rate**.

front_blocks.md: Which conscious activities are controlled by the cerebral hemispheres?

back_blocks.md: Conscious activities including **vision**, **hearing**, **speech**, **thinking** and **memory**.

cards.front_md: Which conscious activities are controlled by the cerebral hemispheres?
cards.back_md: Conscious activities including **vision**, **hearing**, **speech**, **thinking** and **memory**.

front_blocks.md: How do the right and left cerebral hemispheres control the body?

back_blocks.md: The **right hemisphere** controls the **left side** of the body and the **left hemisphere** controls the **right side**. The two hemispheres are joined by the **corpus callosum**.

cards.front_md: How do the right and left cerebral hemispheres control the body?
cards.back_md: The **right hemisphere** controls the **left side** of the body and the **left hemisphere** controls the **right side**. The two hemispheres are joined by the **corpus callosum**.

front_blocks.md: Give two homeostatic processes regulated by the hypothalamus.

back_blocks.md: Regulation of **body temperature** (monitoring blood temperature) and **water balance** (osmoregulation, releasing **ADH** when the blood becomes too concentrated).

cards.front_md: Give two homeostatic processes regulated by the hypothalamus.
cards.back_md: Regulation of **body temperature** (monitoring blood temperature) and **water balance** (osmoregulation, releasing **ADH** when the blood becomes too concentrated).

front_blocks.md: What is the difference between the anterior and posterior pituitary?

back_blocks.md: The **anterior pituitary** produces and releases its own hormones, while the **posterior pituitary** stores and releases hormones made by the **hypothalamus** (e.g. **ADH** and **oxytocin**).

cards.front_md: What is the difference between the anterior and posterior pituitary?
cards.back_md: The **anterior pituitary** produces and releases its own hormones, while the **posterior pituitary** stores and releases hormones made by the **hypothalamus** (e.g. **ADH** and **oxytocin**).

front_blocks.md: Which two control centres are found in the medulla oblongata?

back_blocks.md: The **cardiac centre**, which controls **heart rate**, and the **respiratory centre**, which controls **breathing rate**.

cards.front_md: Which two control centres are found in the medulla oblongata?
cards.back_md: The **cardiac centre**, which controls **heart rate**, and the **respiratory centre**, which controls **breathing rate**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The cerebellum controls heart rate and breathing rate.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Heart rate and breathing rate are controlled by the **medulla oblongata**; the **cerebellum** coordinates movement and balance.

front_blocks.md: Where are the main regions of the brain located?

back_blocks.md: The **cerebral hemispheres** form the large upper part of the brain.
The **hypothalamus** sits beneath them, just above the **pituitary gland**, which hangs below it.
The **cerebellum** lies at the back, underneath the cerebral hemispheres.
The **medulla oblongata** is at the base of the brain, continuous with the spinal cord.

The **medulla oblongata** is at the base of the brain, continuous with the spinal cord.

front_blocks.md: Define **computerised tomography (CT)**.

back_blocks.md: A **CT** scan produces cross-section images of the brain using **x-ray radiation**, showing **physical structures** and any tissue damage.

cards.front_md: Define **computerised tomography (CT)**.
cards.back_md: A **CT** scan produces cross-section images of the brain using **x-ray radiation**, showing **physical structures** and any tissue damage.

front_blocks.md: Define **magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)**.

back_blocks.md: **MRI** uses a **magnetic field and radio waves** to generate high-resolution images of **soft tissue**, useful for identifying damaged tissue and **tumours**.

cards.front_md: Define **magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)**.
cards.back_md: **MRI** uses a **magnetic field and radio waves** to generate high-resolution images of **soft tissue**, useful for identifying damaged tissue and **tumours**.

front_blocks.md: Define **functional MRI (fMRI)**.

back_blocks.md: **fMRI** uses a magnetic field and radio waves to show the **location of oxygenated blood**, allowing **brain function** to be studied in **real time**.

cards.front_md: Define **functional MRI (fMRI)**.

front_blocks.md: Define **positron emission tomography (PET)**.

back_blocks.md: **PET** uses **radioactive tracers** that collect in areas of increased blood flow or metabolism, allowing brain **structure and function** to be studied in **real time**.

cards.front_md: Define **positron emission tomography (PET)**.

front_blocks.md: How does a CT scan produce an image of the brain?

back_blocks.md: A beam of **x-rays** is aimed at the head from all angles and picked up by detectors. **Denser tissue** absorbs more radiation and appears **lighter** on the scan, producing a cross-section image of brain **structure**.

cards.front_md: How does a CT scan produce an image of the brain?
cards.back_md: A beam of **x-rays** is aimed at the head from all angles and picked up by detectors. **Denser tissue** absorbs more radiation and appears **lighter** on the scan, producing a cross-section image of brain **structure**.

front_blocks.md: Why can a CT scan be useful after a patient has had a stroke?

back_blocks.md: Blood is **less dense** than brain tissue, so a CT scan can **locate damaged blood vessels and areas of bleeding**.

cards.front_md: Why can a CT scan be useful after a patient has had a stroke?

front_blocks.md: Give two advantages of MRI over CT scanning.

back_blocks.md: MRI produces **higher-resolution** images of **soft tissue** and does **not use potentially harmful x-rays**.

cards.front_md: Give two advantages of MRI over CT scanning.
cards.back_md: MRI produces **higher-resolution** images of **soft tissue** and does **not use potentially harmful x-rays**.

front_blocks.md: How does an fMRI scan show which regions of the brain are active?

back_blocks.md: It detects the **location of oxygenated blood** by measuring the **ratio of oxygenated to deoxygenated haemoglobin**; active regions receive more blood and 'light up' in **real time**.

cards.front_md: How does an fMRI scan show which regions of the brain are active?
cards.back_md: It detects the **location of oxygenated blood** by measuring the **ratio of oxygenated to deoxygenated haemoglobin**; active regions receive more blood and 'light up' in **real time**.

front_blocks.md: How does a PET scan reveal active regions of the brain?

back_blocks.md: A **radioactive tracer** (e.g. radioactively labelled **glucose**) is added to the blood and accumulates in **metabolically active** regions. The scanner detects areas of **high radioactivity**, showing which regions are active.

cards.front_md: How does a PET scan reveal active regions of the brain?

MRI scans use x-ray radiation to produce images of the brain.

MRI uses a **magnetic field and radio waves**; it is the **CT** scan that uses **x-ray radiation**.

front_blocks.md: Define **neurotransmitter**.

back_blocks.md: A **neurotransmitter** is a chemical that transmits nerve impulses across a **synapse**. Imbalances of neurotransmitters in the brain are linked to some diseases.

front_blocks.md: Define **Parkinson's disease**.

back_blocks.md: **Parkinson's disease** is a brain disorder affecting the **co-ordination of movement**, caused by the **loss of dopamine-producing neurones** in parts of the brain.

cards.front_md: Define **Parkinson's disease**.
cards.back_md: **Parkinson's disease** is a brain disorder affecting the **co-ordination of movement**, caused by the **loss of dopamine-producing neurones** in parts of the brain.

front_blocks.md: Which neurotransmitter is deficient in Parkinson's disease, and what is its role?

back_blocks.md: **Dopamine**, which is involved in **muscle control**. In Parkinson's disease, dopamine-producing neurones are lost, so **insufficient dopamine** is produced.

cards.front_md: Which neurotransmitter is deficient in Parkinson's disease, and what is its role?
cards.back_md: **Dopamine**, which is involved in **muscle control**. In Parkinson's disease, dopamine-producing neurones are lost, so **insufficient dopamine** is produced.

front_blocks.md: Explain how a lack of dopamine leads to the symptoms of Parkinson's disease.

back_blocks.md: **Less dopamine** is released into the synaptic cleft, so less binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. **Fewer sodium channels open**, so depolarisation does not occur, giving **fewer action potentials** and symptoms such as tremors and slow movement.

cards.front_md: Explain how a lack of dopamine leads to the symptoms of Parkinson's disease.
cards.back_md: **Less dopamine** is released into the synaptic cleft, so less binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. **Fewer sodium channels open**, so depolarisation does not occur, giving **fewer action potentials** and symptoms such as tremors and slow movement.

front_blocks.md: How do dopamine agonists treat Parkinson's disease?

back_blocks.md: They **bind to and activate dopamine receptors** on the postsynaptic membrane, producing the **same effect as dopamine**.

cards.front_md: How do dopamine agonists treat Parkinson's disease?
cards.back_md: They **bind to and activate dopamine receptors** on the postsynaptic membrane, producing the **same effect as dopamine**.

front_blocks.md: Define **dopamine precursor**.

back_blocks.md: A **dopamine precursor** (e.g. **L-dopa**) is a chemical that can be **converted into dopamine** in neurones, used as a drug to treat Parkinson's disease.

cards.front_md: Define **dopamine precursor**.

front_blocks.md: Which neurotransmitter is linked to depression, and what does it do?

back_blocks.md: **Serotonin**, which transmits nerve impulses through areas of the brain that control **mood**. **Low levels** of serotonin are linked to depression.

front_blocks.md: How do SSRIs treat depression?

back_blocks.md: **SSRIs** (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) **prevent the reuptake of serotonin** at synapses, increasing the overall level of **serotonin** in the brain.

cards.front_md: How do SSRIs treat depression?
cards.back_md: **SSRIs** (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) **prevent the reuptake of serotonin** at synapses, increasing the overall level of **serotonin** in the brain.

front_blocks.md: How do MAOB inhibitors help treat brain disease?

back_blocks.md: They **inhibit enzymes** that would otherwise **break down neurotransmitters** (such as dopamine or serotonin) in the synaptic cleft, raising their levels in the brain.

Parkinson's disease is caused by producing **too little dopamine**, due to the loss of dopamine-producing neurones.

front_blocks.md: Besides drugs, name two therapies being researched to treat Parkinson's disease.

back_blocks.md: **Gene therapy** (adding genes to increase dopamine production or protect dopamine-producing cells) and **stem cell therapy** (replacing lost dopamine-producing cells).
